message.content:
The title “best jazz singer” is highly subjective and depends on what you value—vocal technique, emotional depth, influence, or innovation. Below is a list of some of the most celebrated jazz vocalists, each known for a distinct style and lasting impact on the genre.  

| Singer | Notable Contributions / Style | Key Recordings |
|--------|------------------------------|----------------|
| **Billie Holiday** | Pioneered the “talking blues” style, emotive phrasing, and a deeply personal approach to standards. | *“Strange Fruit”*, *“God Bless the Child”*, *“Lady Sings the Blues”* |
| **Ella Fitzgerald** | Known as the “First Lady of Song,” her impeccable diction, scat singing, and pure tone set a benchmark for jazz vocalists. | *“Ella Fitzgerald Sings the Cole Porter Song Book”*, *“Summertime”*, *“Misty Blue”* |
| **Sarah Vaughan** | Her rich, operatic voice and wide range earned her the nickname “Sassy.” She blended jazz with blues and pop. | *“Sarah Vaughan with Clifford Brown”*, *“Misty”*, *“The Man I Love”* |
| **Nina Simone** | Though she crossed into soul and folk, her jazz roots and powerful, politically charged performances made her iconic. | *“I Put a Spell on You”*, *“Feeling Good”*, *“Sinnerman”* |
| **Cassandra Wilson** | Modern jazz vocalist who blends jazz with blues, folk, and world music, known for her deep, resonant voice. | *“Blue Light ‘til Dawn”*, *“The World Is Waiting for the Sunrise”*, *“The Blue Room”* |
| **Diana Krall** | Contemporary jazz pianist and vocalist, known for her sultry voice and sophisticated arrangements. | *“The Look of Love”*, *“When I Look at the Moon”*, *“The Girl in the Other Room”* |
| **Tony Bennett** | A master of the Great American Songbook, his warm baritone and impeccable phrasing have earned him a long career. | *“I Left My Heart in San Francisco”*, *“The Way You Look Tonight”*, *“The Best Is Yet to Come”* |
| **Sarah McLachlan** | While primarily a pop/folk artist, her jazz-influenced vocal work and collaborations with jazz musicians show her versatility. | *“Love Will Remember”*, *“I Will Remember”*, *“The Last Time”* |
| **John Coltrane** (as a vocalist) | Though primarily a saxophonist, his vocal experimentation on *“The John Coltrane Quartet”* shows his breadth. | *“The John Coltrane Quartet”*, *“The John Coltrane Quartet Plays”* |
| **Bobby McFerrin** | Known for his a cappella improvisations and vocal percussion, he pushed the boundaries of vocal jazz. | *“Don't Worry, Be Happy”*, *“The Art of the Song”*, *“The Art of the Song”* |

### How to Choose the “Best”

1. **Historical Influence** – Billie Holiday, Ella Fitzgerald, and Sarah Vaughan shaped the early jazz vocal canon.  
2. **Technical Mastery** – Ella Fitzgerald’s scat and Sarah Vaughan’s range are often cited as benchmarks.  
3. **Emotional Depth** – Billie Holiday’s raw vulnerability and Nina Simone’s political conviction stand out.  
4. **Modern Innovation** – Cassandra Wilson and Bobby McFerrin bring fresh perspectives to contemporary jazz.  

Ultimately, the “best” singer is a matter of personal taste and the particular qualities you value most in a performance. If you’re looking for a definitive list, many critics and fans still consider Billie Holiday and Ella Fitzgerald as the top two, but the genre’s richness means there’s always room for new voices to rise.
